Program 2 — Unsupervised Learning: Discovering Tumour Groups Without Labels¶

Owner of this notebook: Naman Singh (240101219) Input: data/breast_cancer.csv (created by 01_data_and_eda.ipynb)

Goal¶

Hide the diagnosis labels and ask: do the 30 measurements contain natural groups, and do those groups match benign and malignant? If they do, the measurements carry the disease signal even before any doctor labels them.

Methods¶

Technique Family Role
PCA dimensionality reduction remove redundancy, visualise 30-D data in 2-D
K-Means centroid-based clustering main clustering method
Agglomerative (Ward) hierarchical clustering builds a tree of clusters (dendrogram)
Gaussian Mixture Model probabilistic (soft) clustering gives each point a probability of belonging to each cluster
DBSCAN density-based clustering finds dense regions and flags noise or outliers

Rule: labels are used only at the end to evaluate the clusters (ARI, NMI, purity), never to build them.

In [1]:
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, AgglomerativeClustering, DBSCAN
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.metrics import (silhouette_score, davies_bouldin_score, calinski_harabasz_score,
                             adjusted_rand_score, normalized_mutual_info_score, confusion_matrix)

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
RANDOM_STATE = 42
FIG_DIR, RES_DIR = Path("figures"), Path("results")
FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True); RES_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
In [2]:
df = pd.read_csv("data/breast_cancer.csv")
FEATURES = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ("target", "diagnosis")]

X = df[FEATURES].values
y_true = df["target"].values          # kept aside, used ONLY for evaluation at the end

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
print("Data used for clustering:", X_scaled.shape, "(no labels)")

Data used for clustering: (569, 30) (no labels)

Why scale? K-Means, DBSCAN and Ward linkage all use Euclidean distance. Without scaling, area (values up to 2500) would decide every distance on its own and smoothness (about 0.1) would be ignored.

1. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)¶

PCA rotates the data onto new axes (principal components) ordered by how much variance they explain. Since radius, perimeter and area are about 99% correlated, a few components should capture most of the information.

In [3]:
pca_full = PCA(random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_scaled)
evr = pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_
cum = np.cumsum(evr)
n90, n95 = int(np.argmax(cum >= 0.90) + 1), int(np.argmax(cum >= 0.95) + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.bar(range(1, 31), evr, alpha=0.7, label="Individual")
ax.step(range(1, 31), cum, where="mid", color="#D1495B", label="Cumulative")
ax.axhline(0.90, ls=":", color="grey"); ax.axhline(0.95, ls="--", color="grey")
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component"); ax.set_ylabel("Explained variance ratio")
ax.set_title("PCA scree plot"); ax.legend(loc="center right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_pca_scree.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

print(f"PC1 explains {evr[0]:.1%}, PC2 {evr[1]:.1%} → first 2 together: {cum[1]:.1%}")
print(f"Components needed for 90% variance: {n90}  |  for 95%: {n95}  (out of 30)")

PC1 explains 44.3%, PC2 19.0% → first 2 together: 63.2%
Components needed for 90% variance: 7  |  for 95%: 10  (out of 30)

X_pca2 = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit_transform(X_scaled)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5))
ax.scatter(X_pca2[:, 0], X_pca2[:, 1], s=14, c="#555", alpha=0.6)
ax.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC2"); ax.set_title("Data projected on PC1–PC2 (what the algorithm 'sees': no labels)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_pca_unlabelled.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

For clustering we use the first components that explain 90% of the variance. This removes noise and redundancy while keeping almost all of the information, and it gives the GMM and DBSCAN fewer dimensions to work in (they struggle in high dimensions, the curse of dimensionality).

In [6]:
pca90 = PCA(n_components=n90, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
X_red = pca90.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print("Reduced data for clustering:", X_red.shape)

Reduced data for clustering: (569, 7)

2. K-Means: choosing the number of clusters k¶

  • Elbow method: plot inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) against k and look for the "elbow".
  • Silhouette score: how well each point fits its own cluster compared with the nearest other cluster (range −1 to 1, higher is better).
In [7]:
ks = range(2, 11)
inertia, sil = [], []
for k in ks:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_red)
    inertia.append(km.inertia_); sil.append(silhouette_score(X_red, km.labels_))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.3))
axes[0].plot(list(ks), inertia, "o-"); axes[0].set_title("Elbow method")
axes[0].set_xlabel("k"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Inertia (WCSS)")
axes[1].plot(list(ks), sil, "o-", color="#D1495B"); axes[1].set_title("Silhouette score")
axes[1].set_xlabel("k"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Silhouette")
best_k = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(sil))]
axes[1].axvline(best_k, ls="--", color="grey")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_kmeans_elbow_silhouette.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
print("k with the highest silhouette:", best_k)
pd.DataFrame({"k": list(ks), "inertia": np.round(inertia, 1), "silhouette": np.round(sil, 4)}).set_index("k").T

k with the highest silhouette: 2
Out[7]:
k 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10
inertia 10062.400 8534.9000 7741.2000 7045.8000 6477.0000 6060.0000 5742.3000 5399.400 5182.900
silhouette 0.371 0.3376 0.3072 0.1866 0.1887 0.1832 0.1733 0.175 0.165

The elbow curve has no sharp knee, which is common with real data, so it alone is not decisive. The silhouette score is clearly highest at k = 2 and drops steadily after that. The data itself suggests two natural groups, chosen without using the labels.

In [8]:
K = 2
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=K, n_init=50, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_red)
km_labels = kmeans.labels_
centers_2d = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_scaled).transform(
    pca90.inverse_transform(kmeans.cluster_centers_))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5))
sc = ax.scatter(X_pca2[:, 0], X_pca2[:, 1], c=km_labels, cmap="coolwarm", s=14, alpha=0.75)
ax.scatter(centers_2d[:, 0], centers_2d[:, 1], c="black", marker="X", s=250, label="Centroids")
ax.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC2"); ax.set_title("K-Means clusters (k = 2)"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_kmeans_clusters.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
print("Cluster sizes:", np.bincount(km_labels))

Cluster sizes: [189 380]

3. Hierarchical clustering (Agglomerative, Ward linkage)¶

It starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two clusters whose merge increases total within-cluster variance the least (Ward). The dendrogram shows the full merge history; cutting it at the largest vertical gap gives the number of clusters.

In [9]:
Z = linkage(X_red, method="ward")
CUT = (Z[-1, 2] + Z[-2, 2]) / 2          # between the last two merges → 2 clusters
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.5))
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode="lastp", p=30, leaf_rotation=90, leaf_font_size=8,
           show_contracted=True, color_threshold=CUT, ax=ax)
ax.axhline(y=CUT, ls="--", color="black", label="cut → 2 clusters")
ax.set_title("Dendrogram (Ward linkage, last 30 merges)"); ax.set_ylabel("Merge distance"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_dendrogram.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

agg_labels = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=2, linkage="ward").fit_predict(X_red)
print("Cluster sizes:", np.bincount(agg_labels))

Cluster sizes: [216 353]

4. Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM): soft clustering¶

GMM assumes the data comes from a mixture of Gaussian distributions and fits them with the Expectation–Maximisation (EM) algorithm. Unlike K-Means, it:

  • allows elliptical clusters of different sizes (full covariance matrices);
  • gives each point a probability of belonging to each cluster.

We choose the number of components with the BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion; lower is better), which penalises extra parameters.

In [10]:
bic = {}
for n in range(1, 7):
    for cov in ["full", "diag"]:
        g = GaussianMixture(n_components=n, covariance_type=cov, n_init=5, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_red)
        bic[(n, cov)] = g.bic(X_red)
bic_df = pd.Series(bic).unstack()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
bic_df.plot(marker="o", ax=ax); ax.set_xlabel("Number of components"); ax.set_ylabel("BIC (lower = better)")
ax.set_title("GMM model selection with BIC"); plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_gmm_bic.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
bic_df.round(0)
Out[10]:
diag full
1 15000.0 15133.0
2 14409.0 14265.0
3 14218.0 14227.0
4 14165.0 14174.0
5 14173.0 14224.0
6 14179.0 14382.0

BIC keeps improving past 2 components because extra Gaussians can always model the long tail of large tumours more finely. For a fair comparison with the other methods (and because both K-Means' silhouette and the dendrogram point to 2), we fit a 2-component full-covariance GMM and look at its soft assignments.

In [11]:
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=2, covariance_type="full", n_init=10, random_state=RANDOM_STATE).fit(X_red)
gmm_labels = gmm.predict(X_red)
gmm_proba = gmm.predict_proba(X_red).max(axis=1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].scatter(X_pca2[:, 0], X_pca2[:, 1], c=gmm_labels, cmap="coolwarm", s=14, alpha=0.75)
axes[0].set_title("GMM clusters (2 components)")
sc = axes[1].scatter(X_pca2[:, 0], X_pca2[:, 1], c=gmm_proba, cmap="viridis", s=14)
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[1], label="confidence = max P(cluster)")
axes[1].set_title("GMM confidence: dark points are uncertain")
for a in axes: a.set_xlabel("PC1"); a.set_ylabel("PC2")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_gmm_clusters.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
print(f"Points with confidence < 0.8 (borderline cases): {(gmm_proba < 0.8).sum()}")

Points with confidence < 0.8 (borderline cases): 52

5. DBSCAN: density-based clustering¶

DBSCAN groups points that have at least min_samples neighbours within radius eps; points in sparse regions become noise (label −1). It does not need k in advance and finds clusters of any shape.

Choosing eps: the k-distance plot sorts every point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour. The "knee", where the curve shoots up, is a good eps. We run it on the first 2 PCs, where density is meaningful.

In [12]:
MIN_SAMPLES = 10
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=MIN_SAMPLES).fit(X_pca2)
kdist = np.sort(nn.kneighbors(X_pca2)[0][:, -1])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(kdist); ax.set_xlabel("Points sorted by distance"); ax.set_ylabel(f"distance to {MIN_SAMPLES}th neighbour")
ax.set_title("k-distance plot for choosing eps")

dbscan_rows = []
for eps in np.round(np.arange(0.5, 2.01, 0.1), 2):
    lab = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=MIN_SAMPLES).fit_predict(X_pca2)
    n_cl = len(set(lab)) - (-1 in lab)
    dbscan_rows.append({"eps": eps, "clusters": n_cl, "noise points": int((lab == -1).sum()),
                        "ARI vs diagnosis": adjusted_rand_score(y_true, lab)})
dbscan_grid = pd.DataFrame(dbscan_rows).set_index("eps")
EPS = float(np.percentile(kdist, 90))   # knee ≈ 90th percentile of the k-distance curve
ax.axhline(EPS, ls="--", color="#D1495B", label=f"chosen eps ≈ {EPS:.2f}"); ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(FIG_DIR / "03_dbscan_kdistance.png", dpi=150); plt.show()

db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=EPS, min_samples=MIN_SAMPLES).fit_predict(X_pca2)
print(f"eps = {EPS:.2f}: clusters = {len(set(db_labels)) - (-1 in db_labels)}, noise points = {(db_labels == -1).sum()}")
dbscan_grid.round(3).T

eps = 1.61: clusters = 1, noise points = 36

      f"{y_true[noise].mean():.0%} (overall {y_true.mean():.0%})")

Malignant share among DBSCAN noise points: 72% (overall 37%)

Insight: DBSCAN does not split benign from malignant. The two groups touch each other with no low-density gap between them, so DBSCAN sees one dense core (mostly benign) and labels the sparse, spread-out points as noise. Those noise points are mostly malignant: DBSCAN works as an anomaly detector that flags unusual tumours. The eps sweep table confirms this: a small eps breaks the data into several small clusters plus hundreds of noise points, and a large eps merges everything into one. No value gives a clean two-group split. This shows when density-based clustering is the wrong tool for partitioning and still useful for outlier detection.

6. Evaluating the clusters¶

Internal metrics (no labels needed):

  • Silhouette ↑ (cohesion vs separation)
  • Davies–Bouldin ↓ (average similarity between each cluster and its most similar one)
  • Calinski–Harabasz ↑ (between-cluster vs within-cluster dispersion)

External metrics (now we reveal the hidden diagnosis):

  • ARI, Adjusted Rand Index: agreement with the true labels, corrected for chance (0 = random, 1 = perfect)
  • NMI, Normalised Mutual Information: shared information between clusters and labels
  • Purity / accuracy: map each cluster to its majority diagnosis and count matches
In [14]:
def purity(y, labels):
    mask = labels != -1
    total = 0
    for c in np.unique(labels[mask]):
        total += np.bincount(y[mask][labels[mask] == c]).max()
    return total / len(y)

results = {}
for name, lab in [("K-Means", km_labels), ("Agglomerative (Ward)", agg_labels),
                  ("GMM", gmm_labels), ("DBSCAN", db_labels)]:
    mask = lab != -1
    internal_ok = len(set(lab[mask])) > 1
    results[name] = {
        "clusters": len(set(lab[mask])), "noise": int((~mask).sum()),
        "silhouette ↑": silhouette_score(X_red[mask], lab[mask]) if internal_ok else np.nan,
        "Davies-Bouldin ↓": davies_bouldin_score(X_red[mask], lab[mask]) if internal_ok else np.nan,
        "Calinski-Harabasz ↑": calinski_harabasz_score(X_red[mask], lab[mask]) if internal_ok else np.nan,
        "ARI ↑": adjusted_rand_score(y_true, lab), "NMI ↑": normalized_mutual_info_score(y_true, lab),
        "purity ↑": purity(y_true, lab),
    }
cluster_eval = pd.DataFrame(results).T
cluster_eval.to_csv(RES_DIR / "unsupervised_metrics.csv")
cluster_eval.round(4)

8. Cluster profiling: what does each cluster look like?¶

We compare the average original (unscaled) measurements in each cluster.

In [17]:
profile_cols = ["mean radius", "mean area", "mean concavity", "mean concave points",
                "mean texture", "mean smoothness", "worst radius", "worst concave points"]
profile = df.assign(cluster=[f"Cluster {c} (≈{names[maj[c]]})" for c in km_labels]) \
            .groupby("cluster")[profile_cols].mean().T
mal_col = next(c for c in profile.columns if "Malignant" in c)
ben_col = next(c for c in profile.columns if "Benign" in c)
profile["ratio (malignant-like / benign-like)"] = profile[mal_col] / profile[ben_col]
profile.round(3)

The malignant-like cluster has nuclei that are much larger (radius, area) and much more irregular (concavity, concave points), which matches the clinical description of cancer cells. Texture and smoothness differ much less. The algorithm found a medically meaningful split on its own.

9. Program 2 vs Program 1: how much do labels help?¶

In [18]:
def scores(y, pred):
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y, pred).ravel()
    return {"accuracy": (tp + tn) / len(y), "recall (malignant)": tp / (tp + fn),
            "precision (malignant)": tp / (tp + fp), "missed cancers": f"{fn} of {tp + fn}"}

rows = {"Unsupervised: K-Means, no labels (all 569)": scores(y_true, km_as_label),
        "Unsupervised: Ward, no labels (all 569)": scores(
            y_true, np.array([np.bincount(y_true[agg_labels == c]).argmax() for c in agg_labels]))}
sup_path = RES_DIR / "supervised_final_summary.csv"
if sup_path.exists():   # written by notebook 02
    sup = pd.read_csv(sup_path, index_col=0).iloc[0]
    rows[f"Supervised: {sup.name} (114 test patients)"] = {
        "accuracy": sup["accuracy"], "recall (malignant)": sup["recall (sensitivity)"],
        "precision (malignant)": sup["precision"],
        "missed cancers": f"{int(sup['false negatives'])} of 42"}
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
for col in ["accuracy", "recall (malignant)", "precision (malignant)"]:
    comparison[col] = comparison[col].astype(float).round(4)
comparison.to_csv(RES_DIR / "supervised_vs_unsupervised.csv")
comparison

10. Conclusions of Program 2¶

  1. PCA: 30 correlated features compress into a handful of components. PC1 alone is an overall "tumour size and irregularity" axis.
  2. The number of groups comes from the data: silhouette, the elbow and the dendrogram all point to k = 2, without using any labels.
  3. K-Means and Ward recover the diagnosis with about 91% agreement (ARI ≈ 0.67), and GMM with about 85%. The disease signal is strong enough that the data separates into benign-like and malignant-like groups on its own. K-Means also has the best internal scores (silhouette, Davies–Bouldin, Calinski–Harabasz).
  4. DBSCAN fails as a partitioner because there is no low-density gap between the classes, but it works as an outlier detector: its noise points are mostly malignant.
  5. Labels still matter: supervised learning (Program 1) is clearly more accurate, especially on the borderline cases where the clusters overlap (circled points above). Unsupervised learning is useful for exploration, pre-screening and finding suspicious cases when labelled data is scarce or expensive.
